l: Joah, The Book of Isaiah
s: Joah, son of Asaph and recorder, accompanies Eliakim and Shebna to meet Rabshakeh, stays silent as commanded, then returns to Hezekiah with torn clothes reporting.

l: Assyrian army (Sennacherib's army), The Book of Isaiah
s: has_casualties 185,000 dead [struck by the LORD's angel] In the Assyrian camp, the LORD's angel strikes 185,000 men dead in a single night. When the men rise early in the morning, all of them are dead bodies. Sennacherib then departs and returns to Nineveh.

l: people on the wall (of Jerusalem), The Book of Isaiah
s: The people who sit on the wall are the audience Rabshakeh deliberately addresses in the Jews' language, warning that they will eat their own dung and drink their own urine. He tells them not to trust Hezekiah and promises them vines, fig trees, and a land of grain and wine if they surrender. They remain silent and give no reply, as the king commanded.

l: gods of the nations, The Book of Isaiah
s: is_a no gods [work of men's hands, wood and stone] Rabshakeh cites the gods of Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, and other countries, saying none delivered their lands from the king of Assyria. He also says they did not deliver Samaria, and uses this to argue that the LORD will not save Jerusalem.

l: Assyrian siege of Judah, The Book of Isaiah
s: Assyria under Sennacherib captures Judah's fortified cities, then sends Rabshakeh with a large army to Jerusalem, where a war of words offers surrender demands and resettlement promises; officials report the threats to Hezekiah, clothes torn.

l: Assyrian blasphemy and threat against Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah
s: is_directed_against LORD [defying the living God] Rabshakeh's words and Sennacherib's letter say that Hezekiah's God will deceive him, that Assyria has utterly destroyed all lands, and that the gods of Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, Eden, Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah failed to save their peoples. The LORD calls this blasphemy against the Holy One of Israel and answers by promising to turn Sennacherib back. The threat ends without any arrow shot at the city.

l: Hezekiah's prayer, The Book of Isaiah
s: Hezekiah prays in the LORD's house, addressing the LORD of Armies as sole God of all kingdoms. He asks him to hear Sennacherib's words, admits Assyria destroyed nations with wooden and stone gods, and requests salvation so all kingdoms know the LORD. Isaiah then relays that the LORD heard and will act.

l: sundial of Ahaz, The Book of Isaiah
s: shadow_moved ten steps backward [as the sign to Hezekiah] The sundial of Ahaz is the instrument on which the LORD causes the shadow, which had gone down with the sun, to return backward ten steps. The sun is said to have returned ten steps on this sundial.

l: Hezekiah's sickness and recovery, The Book of Isaiah
s: Hezekiah's near-fatal illness: Isaiah announces from the LORD that he will die, but after Hezekiah prays the LORD reverses this, and a fig-cake poultice on his boil aids recovery.

l: fifteen added years of life, The Book of Isaiah
s: The LORD, answering Hezekiah's prayer and tears, grants fifteen added years of life, paired with deliverance from the Assyrian king for Hezekiah and the city, and confirms it with a sign.

l: sign (the sundial shadow returning), The Book of Isaiah
s: A sign given by the LORD confirming His promise to heal and deliver: the shadow on the sundial of Ahaz returns ten steps. The sun goes back ten steps where it had gone down, while Hezekiah separately asks for a sign about going up to the LORD's house.

l: Hezekiah's writing (psalm of thanksgiving), The Book of Isaiah
s: authored_by Hezekiah [written after recovering from sickness] The writing records Hezekiah's thoughts when he was sick and after he recovered. It describes his fear of going into the gates of Sheol, his moaning like a dove, and his anguish. It then turns to praise: the LORD has delivered him from the pit and cast his sins behind His back, the living praise Him while Sheol cannot, and Hezekiah resolves to sing with stringed instruments in the LORD's house all his days.

l: Merodach-baladan, The Book of Isaiah
s: Merodach-baladan, son of Baladan and king of Babylon, sends letters and a present to Hezekiah after hearing of his recovery from sickness; his messengers are shown all Hezekiah's treasures.

l: envoys from Babylon (Merodach-baladan's messengers), The Book of Isaiah
s: comes_from Babylon [a country far from Hezekiah] The envoys bring letters and a present from Merodach-baladan to Hezekiah. Hezekiah shows them his whole house of precious things, his armor, and all his treasures, so that they have seen everything he has.

l: Hezekiah's treasures (house of precious things), The Book of Isaiah
s: Hezekiah's treasures include silver, gold, spices, precious oil, and a house of armor, all of which he shows to the Babylonian envoys. Isaiah prophesies that all of it, along with what Hezekiah's fathers stored up, will be carried to Babylon and nothing will be left.

l: Hezekiah's descendants (sons), The Book of Isaiah
s: The LORD declares through Isaiah that some of Hezekiah's sons, whom he will father, will be taken away. They will become eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.

l: Babylonian exile prophecy, The Book of Isaiah
s: A prophecy spoken by Isaiah as the LORD's word: days are coming when everything in Hezekiah's house will be carried to Babylon, leaving nothing, and his sons will become eunuchs in Babylon's king's palace. Hezekiah accepts it as good, since peace and truth will last in his days.

l: the nations, The Book of Isaiah
s: The nations are portrayed as insignificant before the LORD: a drop in a bucket, dust on a balance, less than nothing; their princes and judges are reduced to nothing, withering at his breath.

l: idol (image cast by workman), The Book of Isaiah
s: is_made_by workman [overlaid with gold, silver chains] The idol is described as an image cast by a workman, overlaid with gold by a goldsmith and fitted with silver chains. The poor choose a tree that will not rot and have a skillful workman set up a carved image that will not be moved. It is presented as no answer to the question of whom God can be likened to.

l: grass (metaphor for human frailty), The Book of Isaiah
s: symbolizes all flesh [withers when the LORD’s breath blows] All flesh is likened to grass, and its glory to the flower of the field, which withers and fades when the LORD's breath blows on it. The people are said to be like grass, in contrast to the word of God, which stands forever.

l: those who wait for the LORD, The Book of Isaiah
s: receive renewed strength [mount up with wings like eagles; run and not be weary] Those who wait for the LORD are promised renewed strength, in contrast to youths and young men who faint, tire, and fall. They will mount up with wings like eagles, run without weariness, and walk without fainting.

l: one from the east (raised up by the LORD), The Book of Isaiah
s: A figure raised up by the LORD from the east (also described as from the north, the rising of the sun) and called in righteousness. The LORD hands nations and kings over to him; his sword and bow make them like dust and stubble, and he treads rulers like clay. He calls on the LORD's name. Later he is loved by the LORD, acts against Babylon with his arm against the Chaldeans, and is brought and made prosperous.

l: islands and peoples, The Book of Isaiah
s: reaction fear The islands and peoples are told to keep silent, renew their strength and come near for judgment. When they see what the LORD has done, they fear, the ends of the earth tremble, and they approach. They encourage one another, as the carpenter, goldsmith and smith strengthen each other in making an idol firm with nails.

l: enemies of Israel, The Book of Isaiah
s: Those who rage against and gather to fight Israel are portrayed as disappointed and confounded; they fall, perish, and become as nothing, so that Israel searches for them and finds none.

l: idols and false gods, The Book of Isaiah
s: Idols and false gods are shown to be nothing: in Chapter 41 the LORD challenges them to declare former and coming things or do good or evil. They cannot answer, save, or speak, so they and their works, wind and confusion, are pronounced nothing.

l: judgment of the nations, The Book of Isaiah
s: is_convened_by the LORD [islands and peoples summoned] The LORD calls the islands and peoples to meet together for judgment and opens it with the question of who has raised up the one from the east and worked from the beginning. In the trial he demands that the idols present their strong reasons and predictions, and he concludes that they are nothing, with no counselor who can answer a word.

l: former and new things (the LORD's declared acts), The Book of Isaiah
s: The LORD's declared acts: former things were announced long ago, then done suddenly and fulfilled, denying idols credit. New things are hidden, created now rather than from of old, unheard until today, so Israel cannot claim prior knowledge.

l: Israel's punishment, The Book of Isaiah
s: Israel's punishment is the LORD's judgment on Jacob and Israel for refusing to walk in his ways and disobeying his law. He gives them to robbers, leaving them plundered, snared, imprisoned, and undelivered. His fierce anger sets them ablaze, yet they neither understand nor take it to heart.

l: new thing (the LORD's new act in the wilderness), The Book of Isaiah
s: The LORD tells his people to stop remembering former things because he is about to do a new thing that is already springing forth. He will make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert, giving water to his chosen people so that even jackals and ostriches honor him, and so that the people he formed will declare his praise.

l: sins of Israel, The Book of Isaiah
s: burden LORD [wearied him with iniquities] The LORD says Israel has not called on him, has been weary of him, and has not brought sheep, sacrifices, or sweet cane, but has burdened and wearied him with sins and iniquities. He nevertheless declares that he blots out their transgressions for his own sake and will not remember them, while noting that their first father sinned and their teachers transgressed, leading to judgment.

l: Israel's dispersed children (sons and daughters), The Book of Isaiah
s: Israel's dispersed sons and daughters are called by the LORD's name and created for his glory. He promises to gather them from east, west, north, south and the ends of the earth, commanding north and south to release them.

l: Cyrus, The Book of Isaiah
s: Cyrus is a figure named by the LORD as his shepherd and anointed, called by name though he has not known the LORD. Strengthened to subdue nations and strip kings of armor, he is promised hidden treasures. He will build the LORD's city, enabling Jerusalem's rebuilding and the temple's foundation, and free the exiles without price or reward. Egypt, Ethiopia, and the Sabeans will come to him in chains, acknowledging God is in him.

l: idol makers, The Book of Isaiah
s: Idol makers are declared vain: their delights do not profit and their witnesses neither see nor know. The workmen are mere men, so they and their fellows will be disappointed, confounded and put to shame, with shut eyes and hearts, feeding on ashes, unable to name the lie.

l: idolatry, The Book of Isaiah
s: Idolatry is an abomination and unprofitable; in Chapter 44 a man burns part of a tree for warmth and cooking, makes the rest a god, and begs deliverance, contrasted with the LORD, sole God and Rock.

l: carpenter, The Book of Isaiah
s: shapes tree (the carpenter's wood) [into the figure of a man] The carpenter measures with a line, marks with a pencil, shapes with planes and compasses, and forms wood into the figure of a man to reside in a house. The wood comes from a tree that rain nourished, and part of it is burned for fuel while the rest is made into a god, which the text uses to show the folly of idol making.

l: children of Israel (the barren woman's children), The Book of Isaiah
s: The barren woman's children, promised the LORD's Spirit, will outnumber the married wife's children, spread widely, possess nations, resettle desolate cities, and be taught by the LORD, enjoying great peace.

l: Bel, The Book of Isaiah
s: state bowed down Bel bows down together with Nebo as the text opens. Bel is shown as helpless, since its idols are loaded onto animals and cannot deliver their burden but go into captivity.

l: Nebo, The Book of Isaiah
s: state stooped Nebo stoops and bows down together with Bel. Its idols are carried by animals as heavy loads, are unable to deliver the burden, and go into captivity.

l: idols (of Bel and Nebo), The Book of Isaiah
s: Idols of Bel and Nebo are heavy burdens loaded onto animals and livestock, wearying the carriers; they cannot deliver the burden and themselves go into captivity.

l: god (made by goldsmith), The Book of Isaiah
s: A god fashioned by a goldsmith hired by worshippers who pay in gold and silver; carried on shoulders and set in place, it stays immobile, cannot answer cries, and cannot save from trouble.

l: righteousness and salvation, The Book of Isaiah
s: has_duration forever [salvation to all generations] The LORD says his righteousness is near and his salvation has gone out, and his justice will be a light to the peoples. Though the heavens vanish like smoke and the earth wears out like a garment, his salvation will be forever and his righteousness will not be abolished, lasting to all generations.

l: daughter of Babylon, The Book of Isaiah
s: The virgin daughter of Babylon, also called daughter of the Chaldeans, is a proud, pleasure-loving power once titled tender, delicate and mistress of kingdoms. She sat securely, trusted in wickedness, relied on sorceries and trafficking partners from youth, showed Israel no mercy, and claimed no one else besides her. The records unfold her fall: commanded from her throne into dust, silence and darkness, stripped and shamed, grinding flour, then suddenly struck by widowhood and childlessness in one day, with no savior.

l: astrologers and prognosticators, The Book of Isaiah
s: Babylon's astrologers, stargazers, and monthly prognosticators are challenged to save her, yet are like stubble burned by fire, unable to deliver even themselves, offering neither warmth nor rescue.

l: sorceries and enchantments (Babylon's), The Book of Isaiah
s: is_present_in great abundance [multitude] Babylon's sorceries and enchantments are things she has labored in since her youth, hoping to profit and prevail. They are present in great multitude and abundance, yet the widowhood and loss of children will come on her in full measure despite them. She is told to stand with them, but they cannot save her, and her wisdom and knowledge are said to have perverted her.

l: disaster (coming on Babylon), The Book of Isaiah
s: A sudden, unforeseen disaster announced against Babylon that she cannot put away or understand. It brings desolation, loss of children and widowhood in one day, in full measure, because she trusted her wickedness and said 'No one sees me.'

l: sons of Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah
s: Jerusalem's sons first lie fainted at street heads, full of the LORD's wrath. Later they hurry back as destroyers leave, gather from all around, ask for more room, are carried by nations in bosoms and on shoulders, and the LORD saves them.

l: nations, The Book of Isaiah
s: The LORD will make his servant a light to the nations, and he will lift his hand and banner to them. They will bring Zion's sons and daughters, and their kings and queens will act as foster fathers and nursing mothers, bowing to her with their faces to the earth. Kings also see and rise up, and princes worship, because of the faithful LORD.

l: the speaker (the Lord GOD's servant), The Book of Isaiah
s: The speaker is the Lord GOD's servant, taught and given a tongue to sustain the weary with words. His ear is opened morning by morning, so he is not rebellious and does not turn back. He endures beating, hair-plucking, shame and spitting without hiding. Trusting the Lord GOD as helper, he sets his face like flint, confident he will not be disappointed, and challenges any accuser, since the one who justifies him is near.

l: mother (of the addressed people), The Book of Isaiah
s: was_put_away_for transgressions [of the addressed people] The mother is said to have been put away because of the transgressions of her children. The LORD asks where the bill of her divorce is, implying that no such document exists to show he cast her off permanently.

l: the addressed people (children of the mother), The Book of Isaiah
s: The addressed people, children of the mother, are a rebuked group portrayed across two chapters. First, they are told they were sold for their iniquities, with no one answering when the LORD called; those who fear him should obey the servant's voice, while those kindling their own fires will lie down in sorrow. Then they are called offspring of adulterers and prostitutes, children of disobedience and falsehood. Their sins include idol worship, offerings to smooth stones, killing children in valleys, a bed on a high mountain, and ambassadors sent far away, even degrading themselves to Sheol. Though wearied, they never say 'in vain.' The LORD declares their works will not benefit them, and the wind will carry off their idols.

l: righteous followers (those who seek the LORD), The Book of Isaiah
s: has_in_heart the LORD's law [those who know righteousness] Those who follow after righteousness and seek the LORD are told to look to the rock they were cut from and to Abraham and Sarah. Those who know righteousness and have his law in their hearts are told not to fear the reproach or insults of men, who will be eaten like a garment by the moth.

l: cup of the LORD's wrath, The Book of Isaiah
s: will_be_given_to oppressor [those who afflict Jerusalem; removed from her hand] Jerusalem has drunk the cup of staggering, the bowl of the LORD's wrath, and drained it, leaving her sons full of the LORD's wrath. The LORD declares he has taken it out of her hand so she will not drink it any more, and will put it into the hand of those who afflict her.

l: my people, The Book of Isaiah
s: The LORD's people, who lived in Egypt, were oppressed by the Assyrian and taken away for nothing, mocked by rulers. They are promised redemption without money, will know the LORD's name, and must depart purified, neither hurrying nor fleeing.

l: him who brings good news, The Book of Isaiah
s: A messenger with beautiful feet on the mountains who publishes peace, proclaims salvation, and tells Zion 'Your God reigns!'

l: my servant, The Book of Isaiah
s: The LORD's servant acts wisely and is exalted and lifted very high, though his appearance is marred beyond any man's, astonishing many. He cleanses many nations, and kings fall silent, understanding what they had never been told.

l: redemption, The Book of Isaiah
s: is_achieved_for Jerusalem [by the LORD] The LORD says his people, sold for nothing, will be redeemed without money. The text states that the LORD has comforted his people and redeemed Jerusalem, and that all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of God.

l: the suffering servant (he), The Book of Isaiah
s: The suffering servant is a figure described as the LORD's righteous servant. He grows up as a tender plant without beauty or majesty, despised and rejected, a man acquainted with disease. He is pierced for the speakers' transgressions, bears their sickness, and heals them by his wounds. Silent like a lamb led to slaughter, though free of violence or deceit, he is buried with the wicked and a rich man. Afterward he sees offspring, prolongs his days, justifies many, bears their iniquities, and intercedes for transgressors, counted among them.

l: we (the speakers), The Book of Isaiah
s: The speakers are a confessing people who describe themselves as sheep gone astray, each turning to his own way, unclean, long in sin, and with no one calling on the LORD's name. They also claim to be the LORD's people and the work of his hand. In Chapter 53 they recognize that the servant, once despised, bore their sickness and transgressions, bringing them peace and healing. In Chapter 64 they confess their polluted righteousness, fading like leaves, and appeal to the LORD as Father, asking whether they will be saved.

l: the servant's suffering and death, The Book of Isaiah
s: The servant's suffering is described as bearing sickness and sorrow, being pierced, crushed, bruised, oppressed, and taken away to death, where he was cut off from the land of the living. It is borne for the transgressions and iniquities of others and brings them peace and healing. It is made an offering for sin and is followed by the servant seeing light, being satisfied, and receiving a portion with the great.

l: iniquity and sin, The Book of Isaiah
s: The speakers' transgressions and iniquities are the reason the servant was pierced and crushed, and all have gone astray, each to his own way. The LORD laid the iniquity of all on the servant, who bears the iniquities and sins of many, justifies many, and intercedes for the transgressors.

l: covenant of peace, The Book of Isaiah
s: has_property unremovable [more lasting than mountains] The LORD calls his covenant of peace unremovable: the mountains may depart and the hills be removed, but it will not be removed from the afflicted woman. It is tied to his sworn promise, likened to the waters of Noah, not to be angry with her or rebuke her.

l: everyone who thirsts (addressees of the invitation), The Book of Isaiah
s: They are called to come to the waters and to buy and eat without money and without price. They are asked why they spend money and labor on what does not satisfy, and are told to listen, turn their ear, and come so that their souls will live. They are promised that they will go out with joy and peace, and that nature will sing and clap for them.

l: wicked man (who should repent), The Book of Isaiah
s: A wicked, unrighteous man is urged to forsake his way and thoughts and return to the LORD; if he does, he will receive mercy and free pardon.

l: word of the LORD, The Book of Isaiah
s: The LORD's word goes out from his mouth and, like rain and snow that water the earth and yield seed and bread, never returns empty but accomplishes what he pleases and prospers in its mission.

l: foreigners (who join the LORD), The Book of Isaiah
s: Foreigners who join themselves to the LORD are assured he will not separate them from his people. If they serve him, love his name, keep the Sabbath, and hold his covenant, he brings them to his holy mountain, gladdens them, and accepts their offerings.

l: eunuchs, The Book of Isaiah
s: Eunuchs are told not to call themselves a dry tree. Those who keep the LORD's Sabbaths, choose what pleases him, and hold fast his covenant are promised a memorial and an everlasting name in his house, better than sons and daughters.

l: Sabbath, The Book of Isaiah
s: The Sabbath is the LORD's holy day. Chapter 56 names keeping it unprofaned, with avoiding evil, as a mark of the blessed, and extends the LORD's promises to eunuchs and foreigners who keep it and hold his covenant. Chapter 58 urges honoring it as a delight, not pursuing one's own pleasure, leading to delighting in the LORD and Jacob's heritage.

l: covenant (the LORD's covenant), The Book of Isaiah
s: The LORD declares his covenant with the people: his Spirit on them and his words in their mouths will not depart from them, their offspring, or their offspring's offspring. It is to last from now on and forever.

l: justice and righteousness, The Book of Isaiah
s: The LORD commands his people to maintain justice and do what is right, giving as the reason that his salvation is near and his righteousness will soon be revealed. Holding fast to this is described as bringing blessing.

l: watchmen (Israel's blind watchmen), The Book of Isaiah
s: Israel's watchmen are portrayed as failing guardians: blind, ignorant, mute dogs who cannot bark, dreaming and loving slumber. They are greedy shepherds without understanding, each pursuing personal gain, ending with plans to fill themselves with wine, assuming tomorrow will be as today.

l: the righteous, The Book of Isaiah
s: The righteous, upright and merciful, perish unnoticed; no one considers they are taken away from the evil. Removed from the wicked, they enter peace and rest in their beds, each walking in uprightness.

l: the wicked, The Book of Isaiah
s: The wicked are likened to a restless troubled sea casting up mire and mud, and the chapter closes with the LORD declaring they have no peace.

l: the humble and contrite, The Book of Isaiah
s: The LORD dwells in the high and holy place with those of a contrite and humble spirit, and promises to revive both their spirit and their heart. Those who take refuge in him will possess the land and inherit his holy mountain, and the way is to be prepared and stumbling-blocks removed for his people.

l: idolatrous worship, The Book of Isaiah
s: Idolatrous worship is depicted as including burning with passion among oaks and under green trees, child killing in the valleys, drink and other offerings to smooth stones, and sacrifices on a high mountain. It also includes memorials set behind doors and posts, a bed made into a covenant with others than the LORD, and seeking a king with oil and perfumes. The LORD asks whether he will be appeased by these, and says the gathered idols will be carried away by wind and breath.

l: peace, The Book of Isaiah
s: Peace is what the righteous enter and rest in at death. The LORD creates 'Peace, peace' as the fruit of the lips for those far and near. It is denied to the wicked, for whom the LORD says there is none.

l: healing and restoration, The Book of Isaiah
s: The LORD says he has seen the backsliding one's ways and will heal him, lead him, and restore comforts to him and his mourners. He will revive the spirit of the humble and the heart of the contrite, and says again that he will heal those far off and near. His anger is not forever, since the spirit and souls he made would faint before him.

l: fast (true fast), The Book of Isaiah
s: The true fast is the one the LORD chooses, set against the people's rejected ritual fasting of sackcloth and ashes mixed with pleasure-seeking and oppression. It means releasing wickedness's bonds, freeing the oppressed, feeding the hungry, sheltering the poor, and clothing the naked.

l: oppression and injustice, The Book of Isaiah
s: includes the yoke, finger pointing, and speaking wickedly [to be removed] The people are accused of oppressing all their laborers and fasting for strife, contention, and striking with the fist of wickedness. They are told to remove the yoke, finger pointing, and wicked speech. Ending these is the condition for the LORD's blessing.

l: the oppressed and needy, The Book of Isaiah
s: should_be set free [per the true fast] The oppressed, hungry, poor cast out, and naked are the ones the people are told to free, feed, house, and cover. The text says the people should not hide themselves from their own flesh. Caring for the afflicted soul is tied directly to the people's own blessing.

l: blessings of righteousness, The Book of Isaiah
s: A topic of the blessings the LORD promises for righteousness and obedience: light breaking out like morning, his glory as rear guard, continual guidance, and being like a watered garden. Also riding high places and feeding on Jacob's heritage. Chapter 58 shows obedience bringing healing, answered calls, strength, and rebuilding as Repairer of the Breach.

l: the people (addressed as you/we), The Book of Isaiah
s: A people whose iniquities separate them from the LORD: their hands are defiled with blood, their lips speak lies, and they hurry to shed innocent blood, lacking the way of peace. They confess groping like the blind and knowing their transgressions. Those in Jacob who turn from disobedience are promised a Redeemer and the LORD's covenant, with his words staying in their mouths and their descendants'.

l: Redeemer, The Book of Isaiah
s: will_come_to Zion A Redeemer is promised by the LORD as one who will come to Zion. He comes to those in Jacob who turn from disobedience.

l: iniquity and sin, The Book of Isaiah
s: Iniquities and sins are said to separate the people from God and hide his face so that he will not hear. They are described as bloody hands, lies, conceived mischief, adders' eggs and spider webs that yield no covering, and the people acknowledge that their transgressions testify against them. The LORD's response includes repaying according to deeds, and a Redeemer for those who turn from disobedience.

l: justice, The Book of Isaiah
s: Justice is portrayed as absent: far from the people and turned backward, with truth fallen in the street. Displeased at its absence, the LORD responds by acting himself with his own arm and righteousness.

l: the adversaries and enemies of the LORD, The Book of Isaiah
s: has_fate worm not dying and fire not quenched [loathsome to all mankind] The LORD's enemies are repaid what they deserve by a voice from the city and the temple, and he has indignation against them. He will come with fire, whirlwind chariots, and flames of rebuke, and those slain by him will be many. In the end their dead bodies are looked on, their worm does not die and their fire is not quenched, and they are loathsome to all mankind.

l: nations, The Book of Isaiah
s: serve Zion [nation that will not serve perishes] Nations and kings come to Zion's light, bringing their wealth, serving her, and building her walls, while former oppressors bow at her feet. Any nation or kingdom that will not serve her perishes and is utterly wasted.

l: Zion's sons and daughters (Zion), The Book of Isaiah
s: come_from far away Zion's sons come from far away and her daughters are carried in arms as they gather to her. Ships of Tarshish bring the sons along with their silver and gold. In the end, her people are all righteous, inherit the land forever, and the little one becomes a thousand and the small one a strong nation.

l: Zion's people (Zion), The Book of Isaiah
s: Zion's mourners, described as righteous, are comforted and provided for: they receive a garland for ashes, joy's oil for mourning, and praise's garment for heaviness, then are called trees of righteousness, the LORD's planting, inheriting the land forever.

l: light and glory, The Book of Isaiah
s: is_a light of Zion [has come and risen on Zion] Light and glory rise on Zion while thick darkness covers the earth, drawing nations to her brightness. The sun and moon are replaced: the LORD becomes her everlasting light and her God her glory, so her sun never goes down and her mourning ends.

l: wealth and tribute, The Book of Isaiah
s: comes_from nations [to Zion] The abundance of the sea and the wealth of the nations flow to Zion, including camels, gold, frankincense, flocks, rams for the altar, silver, and Lebanon's cypress, pine, and box wood. These are brought through gates that stay open continually, to proclaim the LORD's praises and beautify his sanctuary. The LORD also promises to give gold for bronze, silver for iron, bronze for wood, and iron for stones.

l: speaker (anointed preacher), The Book of Isaiah
s: An anointed preacher, sent by the Lord GOD, is commissioned to preach good news to the humble, bind up the brokenhearted, proclaim liberty to captives, and comfort mourners. He closes by rejoicing, clothed in garments of salvation and a robe of righteousness, like a bridegroom or bride.

l: the addressed people (Israel, God's priests), The Book of Isaiah
s: The addressed people, Israel, are promised restoration: they rebuild ancient ruins and devastated cities while strangers tend their flocks and fields. They are called the LORD's priests and servants of God, eat the nations' wealth, receive a double portion in place of shame, and their offspring become known and acknowledged as blessed.

l: righteousness and praise, The Book of Isaiah
s: springs_up_before the nations [caused by the Lord GOD, like a bud from the earth] Righteousness and praise are said to be something the Lord GOD will cause to spring up before all the nations. The comparison is to the earth producing its bud and a garden causing its sown seeds to spring up.

l: watchmen (Jerusalem's watchmen), The Book of Isaiah
s: The LORD has set watchmen on Jerusalem's walls. They will never be silent day or night, and those who call on the LORD are urged to take no rest and give him no rest until he establishes Jerusalem as a praise on the earth.

l: salvation, The Book of Isaiah
s: comes_with reward [his reward and recompense accompany it] Zion's salvation is compared to a burning lamp that shines out. The LORD proclaims to the end of the earth that Zion's salvation comes, with his reward and recompense accompanying it.

l: marriage (Zion's marriage imagery), The Book of Isaiah
s: Marriage imagery describes Zion's restoration: her land will be married, and her sons will marry her as a young man marries a virgin. The LORD will rejoice over her as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, and she receives the names Hephzibah and Beulah in place of Forsaken and Desolate.

l: Israel (the people), The Book of Isaiah
s: Israel is the LORD's people, whom he redeemed, saved and carried through the sea and wilderness in days of old. They rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit, so he turned enemy and fought them. The closing prayer laments that Abraham does not know them, their hearts are hardened, their holy people held the land only briefly, adversaries trampled the sanctuary, and they seem never ruled by him.

l: peoples (the LORD's enemies), The Book of Isaiah
s: The peoples are those the LORD trod down alone in his anger and wrath, trampling them like grapes in a wine press so that their lifeblood sprinkled his garments. He made them drunk in his wrath and poured their lifeblood out on the earth, and no one from among them was with him.

l: house (our holy and beautiful house), The Book of Isaiah
s: The holy and beautiful house, where the speakers' fathers praised the LORD, is a sacred place that is now burned with fire, its pleasant places laid waste.

l: sin and iniquity, The Book of Isaiah
s: carries_away the speakers (we) [like the wind] The speakers say they sinned when the LORD was angry and have been in sin a long time. Their iniquities carry them away like the wind, and the LORD has consumed them by means of these iniquities. They ask the LORD not to remember iniquity forever.

l: God's descent and awesome deeds, The Book of Isaiah
s: caused mountains quaking [at God's presence] The speakers beg the LORD to tear the heavens and come down so that mountains quake and nations tremble, as when fire kindles brushwood and makes water boil. They recall that he came down before, did awesome things they did not look for, and the mountains quaked at his presence. They say no one from of old has heard of, perceived or seen a God besides him who works for those who wait for him.

l: rebellious people, The Book of Isaiah
s: A group of rebellious people who walk in their own thoughts and continually provoke the LORD to his face. They sacrifice in gardens, burn incense on bricks, eat pig's meat, and claim to be holier than others. They forsake the LORD, forget his holy mountain, and prepare tables and mixed wine for Fortune and Destiny. Because they did not answer his call, they are destined for the sword, and their name will become a curse among his chosen.

l: servants of the LORD (my servants), The Book of Isaiah
s: The LORD's servants are a spared remnant from Jacob and Judah, chosen to inherit his holy mountains. Unlike the rebellious wicked, they receive food, drink and joy, and are given another name. They build houses, plant vineyards, live long, and enjoy their labor's fruit without toiling in vain.

l: new heavens and new earth, The Book of Isaiah
s: A new heavens and new earth created by the LORD and remaining before him. Former things are forgotten, inhabitants live long lives with no infant dying within days, and God's people rejoice forever, alongside a peaceable holy mountain where nothing hurts or destroys.

l: judgment on the wicked, The Book of Isaiah
s: targets iniquities of the fathers [together with their own] The LORD says it is written before him that he will not keep silence but will repay into their bosom their own iniquities and their fathers' together. Those who forsake him are destined to the sword and bow down to the slaughter, because they did not answer when called and chose what he did not delight in. They will hunger, thirst, be disappointed, cry for sorrow and wail for anguish of spirit, and the Lord GOD will kill them.

l: those who tremble at the LORD's word, The Book of Isaiah
s: has_trait poor and contrite spirit They are the poor and contrite ones to whom the LORD says he will look, and they are addressed as having brothers who hate them and cast them out for the LORD's name. Those brothers' mockery will end in their own disappointment. The trembling ones will see the LORD's comfort, rejoice, flourish like tender grass, and know the LORD's hand among his servants.

l: idolatrous worshippers (who choose their own ways), The Book of Isaiah
s: Idolatrous worshippers who choose their own ways and delight in abominations. Their sacrifices are likened to killing a man or offering pig's blood. Because they ignored the LORD's call, he chooses their delusions and brings their fears, and those eating abominable things end together.

l: nations, The Book of Isaiah
s: The LORD will gather all nations and languages to see his glory. He will send survivors to Tarshish, Pul, Lud, Tubal, Javan, and far-away islands that have not heard his fame, and they will declare his glory among the nations. From all the nations the brothers of his people are brought to Jerusalem as an offering, and the glory of the nations flows to Jerusalem like an overflowing stream.

l: birth of Zion's children, The Book of Isaiah
s: occurs suddenly [before travail, in one day] Zion is described as giving birth before she travailed and delivering a son before her pain came, so that a land or nation is born in one day. The LORD asks whether he who brings to birth would shut the womb, affirming he will not. The birth leads into the invitation to nurse, be satisfied, and be comforted in Jerusalem.

l: judgment by fire, The Book of Isaiah
s: is_executed_by the LORD [by fire and sword on all flesh] The LORD will come with fire and whirlwind-like chariots to give his anger with fierceness and his rebuke with flames. He will execute judgment by fire and by his sword on all flesh, with many slain. The fire is also pictured as unquenchable for the transgressors whose dead bodies are seen, and those who practice abominable rites come to an end together.

l: The Book of Jeremiah
s: This is the book of Jeremiah, 52 chapters of prophecy and narrative centered on Jeremiah, son of Hilkiah, a priest from Anathoth called by the LORD before birth to be prophet to the nations. Despite protesting he is a child, he is made a fortified city and given the LORD's words, ministering under Josiah, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah until Jerusalem's fall. The opening chapters charge Judah with abandoning the LORD, the spring of living waters, for Baal and idols, likening Israel to an unfaithful wife. Repeated calls to return are paired with warnings of an invader from the north, false prophets crying 'Peace, peace,' and condemnation of temple complacency, child burning at Topheth, and injustice. Jeremiah is forbidden to intercede, laments his own persecution, and enacts signs: the ruined linen belt, the potter's clay, the broken container. Kings Shallum, Jehoiakim, and Coniah are condemned, while promises appear of a righteous Branch for David, a regathered remnant, a new covenant written on hearts, and the restored city. The story turns to conflict and siege: Pashhur puts Jeremiah in the stocks, Jehoiakim burns the scroll Baruch wrote, and Hananiah's false two-year promise ends in his death. Jeremiah urges submission to Nebuchadnezzar, writes to exiles to seek Babylon's peace for seventy years, and buys a field at Anathoth as a sign of future restoration. Under Zedekiah he is imprisoned, thrown into a dungeon, and rescued by Ebedmelech. Jerusalem falls, Zedekiah is blinded, and the temple is burned. Gedaliah is made governor but murdered by Ishmael; Johanan and the remnant ignore the LORD's word through Jeremiah and flee to Egypt, taking him and Baruch along, where they keep worshiping the queen of the sky and are warned of judgment. After a word to Baruch, oracles against the nations follow: Egypt, Philistines, Moab, Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, Hazor, Elam, and at length Babylon, whose doom Seraiah is to read and sink in the Euphrates. The book ends with a historical account of Jerusalem's destruction, the deportations, and Jehoiachin's release from prison by Evilmerodach.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Jeremiah is a prophet of the LORD, son of Hilkiah, one of the priests of Anathoth in Benjamin, who receives the LORD's word during the reigns of Josiah, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah. He objects that he is a child who cannot speak, but is touched on the mouth, given the LORD's words, and made a fortified city, iron pillar, and bronze wall against the whole land. He is told Judah will fight him but not prevail, and that people will not listen. The records center on a costly calling. He weeps day and night for his people and wishes to flee to a wilderness lodging, yet is forbidden to pray for them, marry, or enter houses of mourning or feasting. He is compared to a gentle lamb led to slaughter, with enemies among the men of Anathoth seeking his life. He is a man of strife cursed by all, sits alone, suffers mockery and reproach, and is watched by familiar friends for his fall. Still, he says the LORD's word burns in his bones and he cannot stay silent, and he calls the LORD his refuge. He also admits he once interceded for his opponents. His ministry is told through signs and messages: the linen belt, potter's house and container, two baskets of figs, the cup for the nations, and bonds and bars on his neck, which leads to conflict with Hananiah, who later dies as Jeremiah foretold. He sends a letter to the captives in Babylon. He is seized in the temple, put in the stocks by Pashhur, and acquitted with Ahikam's help. Under Zedekiah he is shut up in the court of the guard, buys a field at Anathoth, and predicts the Chaldeans will return and burn Jerusalem. He is thrown into a dungeon, rescued by Ebedmelech, and stays in the court until Jerusalem falls. He dictates his words to Baruch, whose scroll the king burns, and a second is written. After the fall, Nebuzaradan frees him at Ramah and commits him to Gedaliah at Mizpah. The remnant asks his prayer; he tells them to stay, but they accuse him of falsehood and take him to Egypt, where he keeps prophesying at Tahpanhes. He speaks to Baruch, and his final act is writing in a book all the evil to come on Babylon.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The LORD, also titled LORD of Armies and God of Israel, is the central divine speaker of these records. He is presented as the true, living, everlasting King and incomparable creator of heaven and earth, giver of rain, sun, moon and stars, and the one who searches hearts and sees all ways. He is Israel's husband, father and hope, who brought the fathers out of Egypt, led them through the wilderness, gave them the land, and made a covenant requiring obedience to his voice. He delights in loving kindness, justice and righteousness. The records open with his appointing Jeremiah, whom he knew before birth, promising to be with him, and watching over his word to perform it. He then charges Israel and Judah with forsaking him, the spring of living waters, for idols, false prophets, empty sacrifice and injustice. He calls them to return, offering mercy and healing, yet he sends prophets persistently, forbids Jeremiah to intercede, and declares that his planned judgment will not be turned back. He brings disaster from the north, uses Nebuchadnezzar and Babylon as his instrument, hands Jerusalem and Judah over, and rejects child sacrifice as something he never commanded. Even in judgment he says he will not make a full end of his people, and he is weary of showing compassion. Jeremiah is made a bronze wall and is delivered, and individuals such as Baruch and Ebedmelech are spared. Symbols such as the potter, the linen belt and the figs illustrate his sovereignty and his dealings with nations and captives. In the later part he turns to promise: after seventy years he will reverse the captivity, give hope and a future, gather and ransom Israel with everlasting love, make a new covenant, forgive iniquity, and raise up a righteous Branch for David. He also pronounces judgment on Egypt, the Philistines, Moab, Ammon, Edom, Elam and finally Babylon, as a God of retribution and Redeemer of Israel. The records end with his anger as the cause of Jerusalem's fall, his house burned and its vessels carried to Babylon.

l: Jehoiakim, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Jehoiakim is a king of Judah and son of Josiah, portrayed as unjust and defiant toward the LORD's word. He is first condemned for building a lavish cedar house with his neighbor's unpaid labor, and for covetousness, shedding innocent blood, oppression, and violence. He had Uriah fetched from Egypt and killed with the sword for prophesying like Jeremiah. He then cut up and burned the scroll read to him, showing no fear, and ordered Jeremiah and Baruch arrested. The LORD pronounces his end: no mourning, burial like a donkey cast beyond Jerusalem's gates, his body exposed to heat and frost, no heir on David's throne, and punishment for his offspring and servants.

l: Zedekiah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Zedekiah is the last king of Judah in these records, a son of Josiah and son of Hamutal, who succeeded Coniah as king. He began to reign at twenty-one and reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. He did evil in the LORD's sight like Jehoiakim, and neither he, his servants, nor the people heeded the LORD's words spoken through Jeremiah. He rebelled against the king of Babylon. The records center on his wavering relationship with Jeremiah and the prophesied doom that follows from his disobedience. Early on, he sends Elasah to Babylon and sends men such as Pashhur and Zephaniah to ask Jeremiah to inquire of the LORD, hoping Nebuchadnezzar will withdraw. The answers are consistently grim: he is likened to the bad figs and given up with his princes, told to put his neck under Babylon's yoke and live, and warned he will be delivered to Babylon. He imprisons Jeremiah in the court of the guard for prophesying the city's fall, yet secretly consults him, moves him to better conditions with a daily loaf of bread, and orders Ebedmelech to rescue him after yielding to the princes, who he says he cannot oppose. He makes a covenant to free Hebrew servants, and a prophecy says he will die in peace with burnings like his fathers. When urged to surrender, he refuses out of fear of mockery by Jews who defected to the Chaldeans. The end comes with the fall of Jerusalem. He flees by night toward the Arabah but is overtaken in the plains of Jericho and brought to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah. There his sons are killed before his eyes, his eyes are put out, and he is bound in fetters and carried to Babylon, imprisoned until his death. His story is one of a weak, fearful king whose resistance to the prophetic word ends in the loss of his sons, his sight, his freedom, and his kingdom.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Judah is the realm and people, whose capital is Jerusalem and whose kings include Josiah, Jehoiakim, Zedekiah, Jeconiah and Jehoiachin, addressed throughout Jeremiah's ministry. It is first presented as the treacherous sister of Israel: it saw Israel's divorce yet feared nothing, played the prostitute, and returned to the LORD only in pretense. The records stress its deep and persistent sin. The people are rebellious, stiff-necked and unwilling to take correction, with faces harder than rock. They swear by no-gods, trust lying words and the temple, love false prophecy, and commit theft, murder and adultery. They burn incense to Baal, bake cakes for the queen of the sky, and burn their sons and daughters at Topheth. They set up gods as numerous as their cities and altars as numerous as their streets, conspire, and break the covenant. Their sin is engraved on their hearts and altars, and they did worse than their fathers. The LORD repeatedly calls them to turn, including through Baruch's scroll, and they do not listen. Judgment follows: watchers and northern kingdoms attack, the drought brings mourning and languishing gates, and the LORD's anger kindles a fire. Nebuchadnezzar carries off Jeconiah, princes and craftsmen. Zedekiah is condemned and told to submit to Babylon, and its cities become a desolation without inhabitants. Judah is carried away captive, and the treasures of its kings go to Babylon. A remnant and the poorest are left under a governor, and some scattered Jews return. Johanan and the people refuse to stay and flee to Egypt, where they are threatened, with only a few to return. Throughout, promises of restoration run alongside judgment. The LORD says he will not make a full end, and that in those days Judah will walk with Israel and come out of the north to the inherited land. He will reverse its captivity, so that it is a habitation of righteousness, will make a new covenant with Judah and Israel, and will save Judah in the days of the Branch. Its children will seek him weeping, and he will pardon the remnant. The account closes with Zedekiah's fall, Judah's captivity, and Jehoiachin's release from prison in Babylon.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Jerusalem, also called Zion and the daughter of Zion, is the city called by the LORD's name and the central object of his judgment across these records. It is portrayed as filled with oppression, wickedness, and abominations such as adulteries, idolatrous incense, and false swearing. It is unclean, has been a provocation to the LORD since it was built, and is judged in part because of what Manasseh did there. A search of its streets for one just person finds none, though the LORD would pardon it if one were found. The records begin with warnings and appeals. Jerusalem is told to wash its heart of wickedness, and northern peoples are to set their thrones at its gates. It is besieged, its cry goes up in the drought, and no one will pity or mourn it. Its widows outnumber the sand of the seas. The Sabbath command at its gate sets the choice: if the Sabbath is kept, the city will remain forever; if it is violated, an unquenchable fire will devour its palaces. The judgment then sharpens. The LORD declares he will make it heaps, a dwelling place of jackals, an astonishment and hissing, and like Topheth. It will be given into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans, who will burn it. It is the first to drink the cup of wrath, and elders recall Micah's saying that it would become heaps. Jeremiah warns Zedekiah to serve Babylon or see the city become a desolation. Siege ramps are built, the Chaldeans briefly withdraw from fear of Pharaoh's army and are told they will return, and famine leaves no bread in the city. The fall comes in Zedekiah's eleventh year. The city is breached after a siege that began in his ninth year. The Chaldeans burn the king's house, the people's houses, and the LORD's house, and break down the walls all around. Jerusalem is left a desolation, later cited as a warning to those in Egypt. Alongside the judgment run promises of restoration. In those days all nations will gather to it in the LORD's name, it will be called the LORD's Throne and The LORD our righteousness, and it will dwell safely. It will be healed and be a name of joy, praise, and glory before all nations. Left vessels will be restored, and fields near it will be bought again.

l: kingdoms of the north, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The families of the northern kingdoms, called by the LORD, are foreshadowed by Jeremiah's boiling cauldron vision. They come to set thrones at Jerusalem's gates, walls, and Judah's cities, besieging them as the means by which evil breaks out.

l: inhabitants of the land (Judah), The Book of Jeremiah
s: The LORD says evil will break out from the north on all the inhabitants of the land. They are charged with forsaking him, burning incense to other gods, and worshiping the works of their own hands. The people of the land are among those who will fight Jeremiah but not prevail.

l: Baal, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Baal is a false god whom prophets prophesied by and followed unprofitably, while Israel denied pursuing the Baals. Later, Jerusalem and Judah burned incense to Baal on street altars, provoking the LORD to anger and becoming a named cause of the coming evil.

l: Jeremiah's prophetic calling, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Jeremiah's prophetic calling began before his birth, when the LORD knew, sanctified and appointed him prophet to the nations. Though he protested being a child, he is commissioned to go and speak as commanded, set over nations and kingdoms to uproot, destroy, build and plant, and promised divine protection.

l: judgment on Judah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Judgment on Judah is the LORD's announced punishment of Judah and Jerusalem for forsaking him and practicing idolatry, including burning incense to other gods and Baal. It begins with evil breaking out from the northern kingdoms, which besiege Jerusalem and Judah's cities. It then becomes unavoidable: the LORD will not listen to their cries, their gods cannot save them, and the planted olive tree is burned. It culminates in death by sword and famine, unburied bodies, the end of mourning and of mirth and gladness, and exile to an unknown land. Iniquity is repaid double, and nothing is hidden from the LORD. It is likened to a whirling storm bursting on the wicked.

l: Israel, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Israel is the LORD's covenant people, also called Jacob, Ephraim, and the virgin of Israel, and sister to Judah. The records portray it as originally holy to the LORD, his first fruits and firstborn, following him as a bride in the wilderness and held in his hand like clay in a potter's hand. What matters most is the tension between its persistent unfaithfulness and the LORD's refusal to abandon it. Israel forsakes the LORD, digs broken cisterns, and seeks help from Egypt and Assyria. It worships idols and Baal, and its priests, prophets, rulers and fathers all turn away. It is called backsliding, treacherous, uncircumcised in heart, and evil from youth, though it is judged more righteous than treacherous Judah. The account unfolds in stages. First comes remembrance of its early devotion and its subsequent defilement of the land, with a denial of guilt and a warning of shame. Next, the LORD puts it away with a certificate of divorce for its harlotry, yet calls it to return, and its children weep and confess on the bare heights. Judgment follows: lions lay the land waste, Israel is scattered as by an east wind, and it becomes a lost, hunted sheep devoured by Assyria's king and broken by Nebuchadnezzar. It is held captive in Babylon together with Judah, and its wound is called incurable because of its iniquity. Then restoration is promised. The LORD will not forsake it. He is its redeemer, and he will save, heal, multiply and pardon it. He will gather it from the north and all countries, rebuild it, and make an everlasting covenant giving one heart and one way. Ephraim repents and is called a dear son, Rachel's weeping is answered, and the nation will not cease as long as the sun, moon and stars endure. In the days of the righteous Branch it will dwell safely, serving the LORD and David their king, with David's throne never lacking an heir. The final records turn to Babylon, whose slain will fall in return for Israel's slain, and Israel's people are told to flee Babylon and remember the LORD and Jerusalem. The arc runs from holiness through apostasy and exile to promised return and covenant renewal.

l: Jacob, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Jacob, also called Israel, is the LORD's servant, repeatedly told not to fear or be dismayed. Though he faces a time of trouble and captivity, the LORD will save him and his offspring from afar. He will return to live quiet, at ease, and unafraid, with captivity reversed and dwellings shown compassion. Yet he will still be corrected in measure, not left unpunished, though not fully ended.

l: fathers (Israel's ancestors), The Book of Jeremiah
s: Israel's ancestors forsook the LORD, followed, served and worshiped other gods, and broke his law; the present generation is judged worse. Yet the LORD gave their fathers the land and promises to restore the people, while nations say the fathers inherited lies.

l: Egypt, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Egypt is a land ruled by Pharaoh (Hophra), containing Memphis and Tahpanhes, allied with Cush, Put and Ludim, and called an uncircumcised nation. Early on it is the land the LORD brought Israel out of, whose Memphis and Tahpanhes broke Israel's crown; Israel seeks help there and will be ashamed of it, as of Assyria. After Gedaliah's killing, Johanan and the remnant, fearing the Chaldeans, plan to flee there, believing it free of war, trumpet and hunger. The LORD, through Jeremiah, warns 'Don't go into Egypt!' since sword, famine and pestilence will come instead. The remnant goes anyway, in disobedience, and keeps burning incense to other gods. The LORD declares Nebuchadnezzar will strike Egypt, killing or capturing people, burning and carrying off the gods' houses and breaking Beth Shemesh's pillars, and that those dwelling there will be punished as Jerusalem was. Pharaoh Hophra will be given to his enemies. Egypt boasts of rising like the Nile and is likened to a beautiful heifer, yet is incurable, with medicines used in vain. Memphis becomes desolate and Egypt is delivered to Nebuchadnezzar, but afterwards it will be inhabited as in days of old.

l: Assyria, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Assyria is a place Israel turns to, going to drink the waters of the River instead of trusting the LORD. The LORD says Israel was already ashamed of Assyria and will likewise be ashamed of Egypt.

l: Kedar, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Kedar is a people of the east, struck by Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon. The LORD commands the attack, their tents, flocks, curtains, vessels and camels are carried off amid cries of 'Terror on every side!', and they are scattered to all winds with calamity.

l: plentiful land (land given to Israel), The Book of Jeremiah
s: is_a land given by the LORD to the fathers In this place, children, parents, great and small will die and go unburied, and the voices of mirth, bridegroom and bride will cease. The LORD calls it his land and inheritance, which the people polluted with the carcasses of detestable things and abominations, so they will be cast out of it.

l: other gods, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The nations' so-called gods are no gods, made by men, unprofitable lies and vanity. In chapter 2, the LORD notes that no nation changes its gods, yet his people traded their glory for them, calling wood father and stone mother, and he challenges these gods to save in trouble. In chapter 16, serving them causes judgment and exile, after which the nations confess their vanity.

l: Israel's unfaithfulness and idolatry, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Israel's unfaithfulness is an evil, bitter forsaking of the LORD. He charges it with trading him for broken cisterns, prostitute-like worship on every high hill and green tree, and rejecting service. Israel, once a noble vine, became degenerate; its iniquity can't be washed away, despite claimed innocence and forgetfulness.

l: nations, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The nations are a group portrayed negatively in Chapter 10. They are dismayed by signs of the sky, follow vain customs, and are called brutish and foolish for trusting idols. They cannot withstand the LORD's indignation. Accused of devouring Jacob and laying waste his habitation, they do not know the LORD, so the speaker asks that his wrath be poured on them.

l: Israel's idolatry and unfaithfulness, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Israel's idolatry is portrayed as spiritual adultery, prostitution with many lovers on high mountains, under green trees, and with stones and wood. It pollutes the land and brings withheld showers and no latter rain. Israel refuses shame, then confesses shame devoured everything and they disobeyed the LORD.

l: drought, The Book of Jeremiah
s: A drought caused by no rain in the land brings cracked ground, empty cisterns, disappointed plowmen, and suffering animals. It prompts the LORD's word to Jeremiah and the people's prayer, ending with affirmation that only the LORD, not nations' vanities, can send rain.

l: destroyer (the lion from the north), The Book of Jeremiah
s: A lion called a destroyer of nations rises from his thicket and sets out to make Judah's land desolate, its cities laid waste without inhabitants, advancing like clouds with whirlwind chariots and horses swifter than eagles.

l: overflowing waters from the north, The Book of Jeremiah
s: A destructive flood of waters rising from the north, described as an overflowing stream. Announced as evil and great destruction signaled by a standard and trumpet, it sweeps over the land, city and inhabitants, leaving earth waste and void, cities fleeing, and fields a wilderness, while men cry out and inhabitants wail.

l: people of Judah and Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The people of Judah and Jerusalem are a group called by the LORD's name, yet portrayed as foolish, rebellious, and ignorant of him and his law. They are skilled in evil but not in doing good, given to covetousness from least to greatest, deceitful, perpetually backsliding, and unashamed of abomination. They refuse to hear his words, serve other gods, love to wander, and will not return. The account unfolds across five chapters. First, they are urged to circumcise their hearts and lament, since the LORD's anger has not turned back, and leaders will be astonished. Next, they are charged with backsliding and ignorance of the law, unlike migrating birds; their wives, fields, and harvest will be lost. Then they are likened to a ruined belt and to those who cannot change, like the Ethiopian's skin or the leopard's spots, and are to be scattered like stubble. In the drought they confess their sins and plead for his name's sake, but the LORD does not accept them because of their wandering. Finally, because they rejected him and went backward, they are cast out, winnowed, bereaved, plundered, sent with their enemies to an unknown land, and their remnant given to the sword.

l: speaker (the prophet), The Book of Jeremiah
s: has_state anguish [heart trembles at the alarm of war] The speaker protests to the Lord GOD that the people were greatly deceived by promises of peace while the sword reaches the heart. He expresses deep anguish, a trembling heart, and distress at the trumpet and the alarm of war, asking how long he must see the standard. He relates a series of visions of the earth devastated, and hears the voice of the daughter of Zion in travail.

l: wickedness and idolatry, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The wickedness and idolatry of Judah and Jerusalem is bitter and reaches the heart. The LORD calls for abominations and evil thoughts to be cleansed, declaring their own way and doings, and rebellion against him, have caused the coming siege and desolation.

l: prophets, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The prophets are a group characterized by false prophecy and dishonest dealing alongside priests. They are called wind without the word, contrasted with Jeremiah's fiery words, ending with people loving the falsehood and priestly authority.

l: priests, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Priests, allied with prophets, rule by their own authority; they seize Jeremiah, declare him worthy of death for prophesying against house and city, but princes and people reject their claim.

l: wicked men, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Wicked men live among the people of Judah and Israel, lying in wait like fowlers to trap men. Their houses, full of deceit like a cage of birds, made them rich, fat and shining. They neglect the fatherless and needy, and the LORD asks whether he should not punish them.

l: nation from far away (invader against Israel), The Book of Jeremiah
s: A mighty, ancient nation of foreign tongue, whose warriors carry quivers like open tombs. The LORD says he will bring it from afar against Israel, where it will devour harvests, food, flocks, herds, vines and fig trees, and beat down fortified cities with the sword.

l: divine punishment and exile, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Punishment is announced through a lion, wolf, and leopard, through words that become fire devouring the people as wood, and through a foreign invasion. The LORD limits it by promising not to make a full end, and says that because the people served foreign gods in their land, they will serve strangers in a land that is not theirs.

l: northern invaders, The Book of Jeremiah
s: A great nation from the northern country, stirred from the earth's far parts, advances against the daughter of Zion. Armed with bow and spear, riding horses in array, cruel, merciless and roaring like the sea, their report weakens hands and brings anguish.

l: people of Judah (Jerusalem's inhabitants), The Book of Jeremiah
s: The people of Judah, from least to greatest including prophet and priest, are covetous, false, and shameless. They heal hurt superficially, crying 'Peace, peace!', refuse the good old way, the watchmen's trumpet, and the LORD's word and law. They are called grievous rebels, bronze, iron, and rejected silver, and their houses, fields, and wives will pass to others.

l: coming destruction, The Book of Jeremiah
s: A destruction coming from the north country, caused by the people's refusal to listen, is directed at Jerusalem. It begins as a siege that cuts off the daughter of Zion and ruins her palaces, striking every age and relationship. The people respond with terror, sackcloth, ashes and mourning; later news announces it will make Judah's cities a desolation, a dwelling place of jackals.

l: wickedness and oppression, The Book of Jeremiah
s: is_present_in Jerusalem [violence and destruction heard in her] Jerusalem produces wickedness as a well produces water, and violence and destruction are heard in her, with sickness and wounds ever before the LORD. Covetousness, falsehood, slander, and shamelessness mark everyone from least to greatest. The refining process is in vain because the wicked are not plucked away, which is why the LORD brings evil as the fruit of their thoughts.

l: the LORD’s house, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The LORD's house, the temple called by his name, is the site where Jeremiah is commanded to stand and proclaim, and where the people trust 'We are delivered.' Judah's abominations defile it, and the LORD likens it to a den of robbers and warns it will share Shiloh's fate. Worshippers seize Jeremiah there, and princes hear his case at its new gate. Hananiah and Jeremiah speak there after its vessels were taken to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar. Finally Nebuzaradan burns it, and the Chaldeans break its bronze pillars, bases and sea.

l: Shiloh, The Book of Jeremiah
s: was_dwelling_place_of the LORD's name [at the first; later destroyed for wickedness] Shiloh is the place where the LORD caused his name to dwell at the first. The people are told to go and see what he did to it because of the wickedness of his people Israel, and it serves as the pattern for what he will do to the temple in Jerusalem.

l: queen of the sky, The Book of Jeremiah
s: is_a other god [worshiped by Judah in Judah and Egypt] The queen of the sky is the deity to whom the Jews in Egypt, like their fathers, kings, and princes, burn incense and pour drink offerings, and for whom the women make cakes. The people claim they prospered while worshiping her and lacked all things once they stopped.

l: Topheth, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Topheth is a place in the valley of the son of Hinnom where Judah built high places to burn their sons and daughters, something the LORD says he never commanded. In Chapter 7 he declares it will be renamed the valley of Slaughter, a burial ground until no room remains. In Chapter 19 he repeats the burial judgment, vows to make Jerusalem and its defiled royal houses like Topheth, and Jeremiah returns from Topheth, where he was sent to prophesy.

l: child sacrifice, The Book of Jeremiah
s: is_offered_to Baal [burnt offerings in fire] The LORD charges that they built high places of Baal to burn their children in the fire as burnt offerings, which he did not command, speak, or even conceive. It is named among the reasons for the coming judgment on the place.

l: coming judgment and desolation, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The LORD announces coming judgment on Judah: his unquenched anger and wrath will be poured out on this place, on people, animals, trees and crops. He will cast Judah out of his sight, leave unburied corpses as food for birds and animals, and end all mirth and gladness, leaving the land a waste.

l: false trust in the temple, The Book of Jeremiah
s: is_characterized_as lying words that can't profit The people repeat the phrase 'The LORD's temple, the LORD's temple, the LORD's temple' as lying words that cannot profit them. The LORD says they continue in theft, murder, adultery, and idolatry and then stand before him in his house saying 'We are delivered,' so that they may keep doing abominations. He rejects this trust and says real dwelling in the land depends on amended ways and justice.

l: inhabitants of Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The inhabitants of Jerusalem forsook the LORD, burned incense to other gods, refused to hear his words, and sacrificed children to Baal. In Chapter 19 the LORD condemns them with the kings of Judah, foretelling death by sword, corpses as food for beasts, and cannibalism in siege.

l: bones of the dead, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Bones of Judah's kings, princes, priests, prophets, and Jerusalem's inhabitants are to be taken from their graves, spread before the sun, moon, and sky's army, and left ungathered and unburied, lying like dung on the earth's surface.

l: sun, moon, and army of the sky, The Book of Jeremiah
s: is_loved_and_worshiped_by people of Jerusalem [served, followed, sought] The sun, moon, and army of the sky are the objects the people have loved, served, followed, sought, and worshiped. Before them the bones of the dead will be laid out, showing the worship's futility.

l: invading enemy, The Book of Jeremiah
s: An unnamed invading enemy approaches from Dan, heralded by snorting, neighing strong horses that shake the land, then arrives and devours the land, the city, and its inhabitants.

l: speaker lamenting, The Book of Jeremiah
s: A grieving speaker with a faint heart mourns the hurt of his people's daughter, and ends by anguished questions asking why no balm or physician in Gilead has restored their health.

l: backsliding and deceit, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The people's perpetual backsliding is marked by clinging to deceit, refusing to repent, and rushing on their own course like a horse into battle. Deceit also appears in the scribes' false pen, in the prophets' and priests' false dealing, and in the empty cry of 'Peace, peace.'

l: judgment and destruction, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Judgment takes the form of exposed bones, survivors preferring death, loss of wives and fields, and fruitless vines and fig trees. It also comes through an invading army, poisoned water, and serpents that cannot be charmed, and the people confess that the harvest is past and they are not saved.

l: the daughter of my people, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The daughter of the speaker's people is portrayed as deceitful, lying, and disobedient, rejecting the LORD's law and following Baals taught by fathers; the speaker weeps for her slain, and the LORD resolves to melt and test the people.

l: Edom, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Edom, also called Esau, is a nation with cities such as Teman, known for wisdom, and Bozrah. It dwells in rocky clefts and heights, and its heart's pride deceives it. Though small and despised among nations, it is judged: its wisdom fails, hidden places are exposed, and the LORD brings it down, leaving it an uninhabited astonishment like Sodom and Gomorrah, while its orphans and widows are preserved.

l: Ammon, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Ammon is a nation whose capital is Rabbah and whose god Malcam possesses Gad. Rebuked for trusting in its treasures, it faces judgment: Rabbah desolate and burned, Malcam captive with priests and princes, Ammon driven out. Finally, the LORD promises to reverse its captivity.

l: Moab, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Moab is a place and people whose god is Chemosh and whose many cities include Nebo, Dibon, Kerioth and Bozrah. Long at ease from youth and trusting in its works and treasures, it magnified itself against the LORD. Its cities are taken, its people mourn and flee, and Chemosh will shame it. It is destroyed as a people, yet its captivity is restored in the latter days.

l: deceit and treachery, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Deceit and treachery describe the people, Judah, as adulterers whose neighbors and brothers deceive and slander; they speak peace while plotting ambush, refuse to know the LORD through deceit, and thereby incur punishment.

l: coming judgment and desolation, The Book of Jeremiah
s: A divine judgment on a land and its people for forsaking the LORD's law and following the Baals. The land is burned and empty; wormwood, poisoned water, scattering among nations, and the sword follow, until death enters windows and palaces and unburied corpses lie like dung.

l: idols, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Idols are lifeless objects: wood cut from the forest, shaped with an ax by skillful goldsmiths, adorned with silver, gold, blue and purple, and nailed down so they cannot move. They cannot speak, breathe, or do good or evil, and are called falsehood and delusion. The text concludes they will perish in the time of their visitation.

l: inhabitants of the land, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The inhabitants of the land, living under siege, are told to gather their wares; the LORD declares he will sling them out and distress them so they feel it.

l: speaker (lamenting voice), The Book of Jeremiah
s: A lamenting speaker, seriously wounded and bereft, mourns a destroyed tent, broken cords and lost children with no one to restore the curtains. He accepts he must bear grief, admits a man's way is not in himself, and pleads for gentle correction from the LORD, not anger.

l: covenant (LORD's covenant with Judah), The Book of Jeremiah
s: The covenant is the LORD's charge to the fathers at the Exodus: obey his voice to be his people and he their God, receiving a land flowing with milk and honey. Cursing falls on non-hearers. Jeremiah proclaims it because Israel and Judah broke it, bringing its words upon them.

l: men of Anathoth, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The men of Anathoth, hostile to Jeremiah, forbid him to prophesy in the LORD's name on pain of death by their hands. The LORD responds by pronouncing judgment: their young men die by sword, children by famine, leaving no remnant.

l: plot against Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: aims_to cut Jeremiah off from the land of the living [so his name is forgotten] The LORD gives Jeremiah knowledge of a plan to destroy him, which he had not known, in which his enemies say they will destroy the tree with its fruit and cut him off from the land of the living so his name is remembered no more. Jeremiah brings his cause to the LORD, who responds by pronouncing punishment on the men of Anathoth who seek his life.

l: the wicked, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The wicked are a group planted and rooted by the LORD, flourishing and bearing fruit, yet treacherous, honoring Him with their mouths while their hearts stay far away; the speaker asks that they be pulled out like sheep for slaughter.

l: speaker (the complainant to the LORD), The Book of Jeremiah
s: The speaker contends with the LORD, asking why the way of the wicked prospers, and says the LORD knows and tests his heart. The LORD replies that he has been wearied by footmen and cannot yet contend with horses, and that his brothers and father's house have dealt treacherously with him, so he should not believe their beautiful words.

l: heritage (the LORD's heritage), The Book of Jeremiah
s: The LORD's heritage, his dearly beloved, has been cast off and given into the hand of her enemies. She has become to him like a lion in the forest that uttered her voice against him, and he says he hated her. She is also likened to a speckled bird of prey surrounded by birds of prey, with animals assembled to devour her, and to a vineyard trodden by many shepherds and made a desolate wilderness.

l: the land, The Book of Jeremiah
s: A land mourns the wickedness of its inhabitants: herbs wither, animals and birds perish, and no one cares. Destroyers and the LORD's sword devour it end to end, leaving it desolate, with wheat sown but thorns reaped.

l: evil neighbors, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The evil neighbors are nations that touch the inheritance the LORD gave Israel. He will pluck them from their land, and Judah from among them, then return with compassion and restore each. If they learn his people's ways and swear by his name, they will be built up; a nation refusing to hear will be destroyed.

l: the prosperity of the wicked, The Book of Jeremiah
s: is questioned by the speaker [speaker asks why it happens] The speaker raises it as the central question: why the way of the wicked prospers and the treacherous are at ease. It is described as the LORD's own planting, with the wicked taking root, growing and bearing fruit, though only in word and not in heart. The speaker asks that they be pulled out for the day of slaughter, and the LORD's reply speaks of wheat sown yielding thorns and of fruits to be ashamed of.

l: linen belt (Jeremiah's belt), The Book of Jeremiah
s: A linen belt is bought, worn unwashed on the waist, then hidden in a rock cleft by the Euphrates. Retrieved after many days, it is ruined and profitable for nothing, symbolizing how the LORD will ruin Judah's pride and evil people, while also picturing Israel and Judah clinging to him.

l: Euphrates, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The Euphrates is the place where the narrator is sent to hide the belt in a cleft of the rock. He returns there after many days and digs up the ruined belt.

l: David, The Book of Jeremiah
s: David is a servant of the LORD. The LORD promises a righteous Branch will grow for him, that he will never lack a man on Israel's throne, and that his offspring will multiply like the sky's stars and sea's sand.

l: pride, The Book of Jeremiah
s: is_condemned_by the LORD [Jeremiah weeps over it] Pride is the fault the LORD says he will ruin in Judah and Jerusalem, as shown by the ruined belt. The people are urged not to be proud and to give glory to the LORD, and the narrator weeps in secret for their pride. The king and queen mother are told to humble themselves because their crowns of glory have come down.

l: drunkenness and destruction (judgment), The Book of Jeremiah
