s: The LORD says every container should be filled with wine and applies this to filling the inhabitants of the land, including kings, priests, prophets, and all of Jerusalem, with drunkenness. He will dash fathers and sons against one another, without pity, sparing, or compassion. Further judgment includes darkness, scattering like stubble, and the exposure of Jerusalem's shame.

l: captivity, The Book of Jeremiah
s: befalls flock (the LORD's flock) The narrator weeps because the LORD's flock has been taken captive. Judah is said to be carried away captive, all of them wholly, and the cities of the South are shut up. A foe is seen coming from the north, and the king and queen mother are asked where the beautiful flock given to them has gone.

l: false prophets, The Book of Jeremiah
s: False prophets are those the LORD never sent, commanded, or spoke to. They prophesy lying visions, divination, and deceit of their own heart, assuring the people of peace and no sword or famine. The LORD decrees they will themselves be consumed by sword and famine.

l: sword, famine, and pestilence, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Sword, famine, and pestilence are the LORD's instruments of punishment on Judah. In Chapter 14 he vows to consume the people with them, false prophets who deny them will die by them, and corpses will lie unburied. In Chapter 44 they are the means that punished Jerusalem and will consume the remnant in Egypt, making them a horror, curse, and reproach.

l: sins of the people, The Book of Jeremiah
s: are many [rebellions testify against them] The people's iniquities and many rebellions are said to testify against them, and the LORD says he will remember their iniquity and punish their sins. He says he will pour their wickedness on them. The people themselves acknowledge their wickedness and the iniquity of their fathers, confessing they have sinned against the LORD.

l: persecutors (of Jeremiah), The Book of Jeremiah
s: Jeremiah's familiar friends defame him and watch for his fall to take revenge; Jeremiah declares the LORD will make them stumble, fail to prevail, and suffer everlasting dishonor, and asks to witness vengeance.

l: judgment of death, sword, famine, and captivity, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The LORD assigns each to its appointed fate: those for death to death, for the sword to the sword, for famine to famine, and for captivity to captivity. He appoints four kinds of destroyers: the sword to kill, dogs to tear, and the birds of the sky and animals of the earth to devour and destroy.

l: Jeremiah's suffering and complaint, The Book of Jeremiah
s: is_described_as perpetual pain and incurable wound Jeremiah cries woe that he was born a man of strife, cursed by all, and says he has suffered reproach for the LORD's sake and sat alone filled with indignation. He asks why his pain is perpetual and his wound incurable, and whether the LORD will be to him a deceitful brook. The LORD answers with a call to return and a promise of protection and rescue.

l: people of Judah (this people), The Book of Jeremiah
s: The people of Judah are accused of sinning worse than their fathers by following stubborn evil hearts, not listening, and polluting the land with detestable things. Judgment follows: grievous deaths by sword and famine without burial or mourning, and joy ceasing. They will be cast out to an unknown foreign land, serving other gods there, repaid double.

l: foreign land of exile, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The LORD says he will cast the people into a land that neither they nor their fathers have known. There they will serve other gods day and night and receive no favor from him.

l: restoration of Israel (return from exile), The Book of Jeremiah
s: The LORD promises to restore Israel and Judah from exile, an act of deliverance so great it will surpass the Exodus in memory. Recompense for sin comes first. He then reverses their captivity, sends fishermen and hunters to gather them from the north country and the ends of the earth, and brings them to the land given their fathers, while their oppressors go into captivity. The gathering includes the blind, lame, and women with child, weeping but led by rivers in a straight way. They sing on Zion, enjoy grain, wine, and oil, and see mourning turned to joy. The city is rebuilt and made holy, never again plucked up.

l: Sabbath day, The Book of Jeremiah
s: is_to_be holy [no burden or work; commanded to fathers] The Sabbath day is to be made holy by bearing no burden out of houses or through Jerusalem's gates and doing no work, as the LORD commanded their fathers. The people did not listen but stiffened their necks. Keeping it brings lasting blessing for the city, while breaking it brings an unquenched fire.

l: Sin of Judah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The sin of Judah is a permanent, indelible guilt, written with an iron pen and diamond point on their hearts and altar horns. Tied to altars and Asherah poles on high hills, it brings plunder of treasures and high places, loss of heritage, and the LORD's unending anger.

l: man who trusts in man, The Book of Jeremiah
s: A cursed man who relies on the strength of flesh while his heart departs from the LORD. He is likened to a desert bush that never sees good come, dwelling in parched, uninhabited salt land.

l: man who trusts in the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah
s: A man who trusts in the LORD is blessed. He is likened to a tree planted by water with roots by the river, unafraid in heat, green in drought, and never ceasing to bear fruit.

l: potter (potter's house), The Book of Jeremiah
s: has_authority_over clay vessel (potter's vessel) [remakes it as seems good to him] The potter is seen by Jeremiah at his house working on the wheels. When the vessel he is making is marred in his hand, he makes it again into another vessel as seems good to him, which the LORD uses as an image of his own right over Israel.

l: clay vessel (potter's vessel), The Book of Jeremiah
s: has_state marred [in the potter's hand] The vessel made of clay is marred in the potter's hand, and the potter makes it again into another vessel as seems good to him. It serves as the image of the house of Israel in the LORD's hand.

l: men of Judah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The men of Judah, with Jerusalem's inhabitants, are a stubborn group targeted by the LORD, who frames evil against them. Told to turn from evil ways and amend their doings, they reject the call as vain and resolve to follow their own plans and evil hearts.

l: inhabitants of Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah
s: disobeys the LORD [has not listened despite repeated warnings] The men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem are accused of refusing instruction and not heeding the LORD, who rose early to speak to them and sent the prophets calling them to turn from evil and from other gods. Unlike the Rechabites, they have not listened, and the LORD announces that he will bring on them all the evil he pronounced.

l: nation (any nation spoken of by the LORD), The Book of Jeremiah
s: is_subject_to the LORD [he may repent of evil or good depending on its conduct] The LORD says that when he speaks of plucking up, breaking down, and destroying a nation or kingdom, he will repent of the evil he planned if that nation turns from its evil. When he speaks of building and planting a nation, he will repent of the good he promised if it does evil and does not obey his voice.

l: Jeremiah's opponents, The Book of Jeremiah
s: A group opposing Jeremiah, confident that law, counsel, and word will never perish from priest, wise, and prophet. They plot to strike him with the tongue and ignore his words, and Jeremiah says they have dug a pit and hidden snares to kill him.

l: potter’s earthen container (Jeremiah's purchase), The Book of Jeremiah
s: symbolizes breaking of the people and city [cannot be made whole again] The LORD tells Jeremiah to buy it and take it to the valley of the son of Hinnom. Jeremiah is to break it in the sight of the men with him, as a sign that the LORD will break this people and city so that it cannot be made whole again.

l: valley of the son of Hinnom, The Book of Jeremiah
s: A place by the gate Harsith where Jeremiah is sent to proclaim the LORD's words; as judgment, the LORD declares it will be renamed the valley of Slaughter.

l: siege and cannibalism judgment, The Book of Jeremiah
s: A divine judgment on Judah and Jerusalem: the LORD declares that during enemy siege and distress, people will be driven to eat the flesh of their sons, daughters and friends, as announced in Chapter 19.

l: Pashhur, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Pashhur is a priest and chief officer in the LORD's house, son of Immer. He strikes Jeremiah and puts him in the stocks, then releases him. Jeremiah renames him Magormissabib and prophesies terror, captivity in Babylon, and death and burial there, because he prophesied falsely to his friends.

l: king of Babylon, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The king of Babylon is a feared foreign ruler in Jeremiah's prophecies. In Chapter 20 the LORD says he will receive all Judah and carry people captive to Babylon, killing some by sword. In Chapter 38 his army is to take Jerusalem, threatening Zedekiah and the royal women. In Chapter 42 the remnant fears him, but the LORD twice says not to be afraid, promising salvation, mercy, and return to their land.

l: Babylon, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Babylon is a land and kingdom of the Chaldeans, on the Euphrates, ruled by King Nebuchadnezzar and worshipping the deities Bel and Merodach. Across the records it is both the LORD's instrument of judgment and the object of that judgment. Its story runs in three stages. First, Babylon is the destination of captivity. Judah's people, treasures, and temple vessels are carried there, including Pashhur, Jeconiah, and Zedekiah, whose sons and princes are killed before he is imprisoned in Babylon. The LORD gives the nations to Nebuchadnezzar, and they serve him seventy years. Jeremiah rejects Hananiah's claim of a quick return, and the exiles are told to seek Babylon's peace and pray for it, since in its peace they will have peace. Babylon's king appoints Gedaliah governor over those left in Judah, besieges Jerusalem, and carries off the bronze of the LORD's house. Later Evilmerodach releases Jehoiachin. Second, after the seventy years the LORD will punish the king and nation for their iniquity. Third, the closing oracles in chapters 50 and 51 declare Babylon taken and fallen. It was a golden cup in the LORD's hand that made the earth drunk and a hammer of the whole earth, now cut apart and broken. It is condemned for pride against the LORD, for plundering his heritage, for devouring Zion, and for mad devotion to engraved images. Its idols are dismayed, its walls, gates, and mighty men are overthrown, and its king grows feeble. Its fate, decreed by the LORD, is desolation without inhabitants, like Sodom and Gomorrah, a dwelling for jackals, forever.

l: Jeremiah's prophecy of Babylonian conquest, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Jeremiah declares in the LORD's name that all Judah will be given to the king of Babylon, with its people killed or taken captive and its treasures carried off to Babylon. He applies it personally to Pashhur, who will die in Babylon with his household and friends. The prophecy is what provoked Pashhur to put Jeremiah in the stocks.

l: Jeremiah's lament, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Jeremiah's lament in Chapter 20: overpowered by the LORD, he is mocked daily for proclaiming violence and destruction, yet cannot stay silent because the LORD's word burns like fire in his bones. It ends cursing his birth day and its announcer, asking why he left the womb.

l: Nebuchadnezzar, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Nebuchadnezzar is the king of Babylon, presented throughout these records as a powerful ruler and as the LORD's servant, an instrument of judgment. He commands a large army that includes the kingdoms and peoples under his dominion, and many nations are said to be under his yoke. They are to serve him, his son, and his son's son until the time of his own land comes, and any nation that refuses is to be punished until consumed by his hand. The records open with him making war on Zedekiah and Jerusalem. The LORD declares he will give Zedekiah and the city into Nebuchadnezzar's hand and that the city will be burned. He is dated against Jehoiakim's reign, and his first year matches Jehoiakim's fourth. In that same fourth year he strikes Pharaoh Necoh's army at Carchemish. He is said to have taken the vessels of the LORD's house to Babylon and to have carried the Judeans away captive. Hananiah falsely claims his yoke will be broken in two years, but the LORD says the nations will serve him. The LORD also says Ahab and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah will be delivered into his hand and killed. He besieges Jerusalem in Zedekiah's ninth year and builds forts around it. At Riblah he pronounces judgment on Zedekiah, killing Zedekiah's sons and all the nobles of Judah. He orders Nebuzaradan to care for Jeremiah and do him no harm. Nebuzaradan enters Jerusalem in his nineteenth year, and deportations are dated by his seventh, eighteenth and twenty-third years. Further prophecies say he struck Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor. He will set his throne on hidden stones at Tahpanhes and strike Egypt, burn the houses of its gods, and leave in peace. Overall he is a conqueror who carries out the LORD's judgment on Judah, Egypt and the surrounding nations.

l: Chaldeans, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The Chaldeans are the people of Babylon, fighting for Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and appearing throughout the records chiefly as the besieging army against Jerusalem. Early on they surround the city, build siege ramps, and are told by the LORD to be the ones to whom defenders may surrender and live. They withdraw briefly when Pharaoh's army approaches, but the LORD says they will return, take the city, and burn it. Jeremiah is accused of defecting to them, and he warns Zedekiah that the city will burn if he does not surrender. The siege ends with the Chaldean army pursuing and overtaking Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho, bringing him to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah, burning the houses, breaking down Jerusalem's walls, and carrying the temple's bronze to Babylon. Afterward, Ishmael kills Chaldean men at Mizpah along with Gedaliah, the governor the king of Babylon appointed, and Johanan's people fear the Chaldeans, which motivates their plan to go to Egypt. The records close with prophecies reversing their fortune: a sword will fall on Chaldea and Babylon, the land will be plundered, and the Chaldeans will be repaid for the evil they did in Zion.

l: House of David, The Book of Jeremiah
s: is_commanded_by the LORD [to execute justice in the morning and deliver the robbed] The house of the king of Judah is told to execute justice in the morning and deliver the robbed from the hand of the oppressor. Otherwise the LORD's wrath will go out like an unquenchable fire because of the evil of their doings. The LORD says he will punish them according to the fruit of their doings.

l: people of the city (Zedekiah's people), The Book of Jeremiah
s: faces_choice_of way of life and the way of death [set before them by the LORD] The people are told that those who remain in the city will die by the sword, famine, and pestilence. Those who go out to the besieging Chaldeans will live. Those left after the pestilence will be delivered into Nebuchadnezzar's hand and struck down without mercy.

l: siege of Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The siege of Jerusalem was a Babylonian assault fought by the Chaldeans, conducted by Nebuchadnezzar's army in Zedekiah's tenth year (Nebuchadnezzar's eighteenth), also against Judah's other fortified cities such as Lachish and Azekah. Siege ramps were built, and Zedekiah hoped the LORD would force a withdrawal. The LORD instead declared he would fight against the city and give it to Babylon to be burned. Jeremiah linked it to sword, famine, and pestilence. When the Chaldeans briefly withdrew on news of Pharaoh's army, the LORD said it was temporary: they would return, take, and burn the city, as bread ran short.

l: pestilence, sword, and famine, The Book of Jeremiah
s: will_strike people of the city (Zedekiah's people) [pestilence first, then sword and famine] The LORD says he will strike the inhabitants of the city, both man and animal, with a great pestilence. Those who remain in the city are said to die by the sword, famine, and pestilence. Survivors of these are to be delivered into Nebuchadnezzar's hand.

l: way of life and the way of death, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The LORD offers the people two choices: remain in the besieged city and die by sword, famine, and pestilence, or go out to the Chaldeans and survive with their lives.

l: king of Judah (house of the king of Judah), The Book of Jeremiah
s: The king of Judah, who sits on David's throne, is told to hear the LORD's word along with his servants and people. If they do justice, kings will keep entering the gates on chariots and horses; if not, the house will become a desolation.

l: house of the king of Judah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The house of the king of Judah, likened by the LORD to Gilead and Lebanon's head, is doomed to become a wilderness: destroyers will fell its cedars, and nations will learn it fell for abandoning the covenant.

l: Shallum, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Shallum, son of Josiah, became king of Judah in his father's place. He was led away captive, and the LORD declares he will never return or see the land again, dying in captivity; people should weep for him.

l: Coniah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Coniah is a king of Judah, son of Jehoiakim, made king by Nebuchadnezzar. He is pronounced doomed: given into the hands of those seeking his life, cast out with his mother to die in a foreign land, never returning home, and recorded as childless, with no offspring prospering on David's throne.

l: justice and righteousness, The Book of Jeremiah
s: was_practiced_by Josiah [it was well with him] The LORD commands the king's house to execute justice and righteousness, deliver the robbed from the oppressor, and not wrong foreigners, the fatherless, or widows. Josiah is cited as having done justice and righteousness, so that it was well with him, and judging the cause of the poor and needy is described as knowing the LORD.

l: unjust house-building, The Book of Jeremiah
s: is_condemned_by the LORD [builds by unrighteousness and injustice, using neighbor's service without wages] The LORD pronounces woe on one who builds his house by unrighteousness and his rooms by injustice, using his neighbor's service without wages. It is exemplified by a wide house with cedar ceiling painted red, and the LORD asks whether excelling in cedar justifies reigning.

l: shepherds (of the LORD's flock), The Book of Jeremiah
s: has_situation scattered and driven away the flock [condemned by the LORD] The shepherds are accused of destroying and scattering the LORD's flock, driving them away and not visiting them, and the LORD says he will visit on them the evil of their doings. He promises to set up other shepherds over the flock who will feed them so that none will be afraid, dismayed, or lacking.

l: flock (the LORD's people), The Book of Jeremiah
s: The LORD's flock, scattered into many countries by its shepherds and misled by prophets' false dreams and lies, is promised regathering of its remnant to their folds, where it will be fruitful and multiply.

l: righteous Branch (of David), The Book of Jeremiah
s: A righteous Branch the LORD promises to raise for David. He reigns as a wise king and executes justice and righteousness in the land. In his days Judah is saved and Israel dwells safely. He is called 'The LORD our righteousness.' The promise appears in Chapter 23 and is repeated in Chapter 33.

l: prophets, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The prophets are a group condemned as profane, speaking visions from their own hearts rather than the LORD. Unsent and absent from his council, those of Samaria and Jerusalem prophesy by Baal, commit adultery, lie, and strengthen evildoers; the LORD opposes them, vowing wormwood and poisoned water.

l: false dreams, The Book of Jeremiah
s: are_told_by prophets [cause the people to err; not sent by the LORD] The prophets claim 'I had a dream!' and tell lying dreams in the LORD's name, which the LORD says come from the deceit of their own hearts. He says these dreams aim to make his people forget his name as their fathers did because of Baal, that they cause the people to err, and that they profit the people not at all.

l: the LORD's word, The Book of Jeremiah
s: is_like fire [also like a hammer breaking rock] The LORD contrasts a mere dream with his word as straw is to wheat, and says his word is like fire and like a hammer that breaks rock in pieces. A prophet who has his word is to speak it faithfully, while those who steal it or say 'He says' are condemned.

l: the message from the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah
s: is_forbidden_phrase the LORD [people may no longer mention it] The phrase 'the message from the LORD' is forbidden because every man's own word has become his message, perverting the words of the living God. The LORD says that anyone who uses the phrase will be punished along with his household, and that those who persist will be forgotten and cast off from his presence.

l: good figs, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Very good, first-ripe figs in one basket, symbolizing Judah's captives sent to the Chaldeans, whom the LORD regards as good.

l: bad figs, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Bad figs are a basket of inedible, very bad figs; symbolically they represent Zedekiah, his princes, Jerusalem's remnant, and those in Egypt, whom the LORD will give up to judgment.

l: captives of Judah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The captives of Judah, sent by the LORD into the land of the Chaldeans, are regarded as good, likened to good figs. The LORD promises to watch over them for good, return them to the land, build and plant them, and give them a heart to know him, making them his people.

l: remnant of Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The remnant of Jerusalem remaining in the land is likened to bad figs; the LORD gives them up, tossing them among kingdoms through sword, famine, and pestilence until consumed from the land.

l: cup of the wine of wrath, The Book of Jeremiah
s: A cup given by the LORD to Jeremiah, which all nations must drink; it makes them reel, go insane and fall by the sword, refusals are overruled, and the king of Sheshach drinks last.

l: nations (under Nebuchadnezzar's yoke), The Book of Jeremiah
s: A collective of nations, from Egypt, Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon to Elam and the Medes, is made to drink the cup of judgment. They must serve Nebuchadnezzar, his son, and his son's son for seventy years. Those who submit remain and till their land; those who refuse face sword, famine, and pestilence. Eventually, many nations and great kings will make Babylon's king their bondservant.

l: Philistines, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The Philistines, a group with cities Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron and a remnant of Ashdod, are the remnant of Caphtor; the LORD tells Jeremiah a day comes to destroy them all and cut off Tyre and Sidon's helpers.

l: Ashkelon, The Book of Jeremiah
s: has_state brought to nothing Ashkelon is said to be brought to nothing. It is also the target against which the LORD has appointed his sword, along with the seashore.

l: Gaza, The Book of Jeremiah
s: has_state baldness [mourning] Gaza is named as the place Pharaoh struck, which dates the word to Jeremiah. Baldness is said to have come on Gaza.

l: Elam, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Elam, a people and land whose chief strength is its bow, is condemned in a word to Jeremiah: the LORD will break its bow, scatter its people to every nation, destroy its king and princes, then reverse its captivity in the latter days.

l: Medes, The Book of Jeremiah
s: has_purpose_stirred_by the LORD [against Babylon] The LORD has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes, along with their governors and deputies, to be prepared against Babylon. Their rising fulfills his purpose to destroy it as vengeance for his temple.

l: seventy years, The Book of Jeremiah
s: is_a duration of the nations' service to Babylon The LORD states that after seventy years are accomplished for Babylon, he will visit the exiles and perform his good word. This will cause them to return to Jerusalem. The period frames the long stay in Babylon that the letter tells them to settle into.

l: divine judgment on the nations, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The LORD's controversy with the nations: judgment on all flesh, beginning at Jerusalem, the city called by his name. The sword is sent on all earth's inhabitants; evil spreads nation to nation like a great storm, the slain fill the earth, and shepherds find no escape.

l: Judah's disobedience, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Judah's disobedience is its refusal to heed Jeremiah and the prophets for twenty-three years, persisting in serving and worshipping other gods, provoking the LORD to anger with its own handiwork, which is the stated reason for coming judgment.

l: prophets, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The prophets join the priests and people in seizing Jeremiah and declaring him worthy of death for prophesying against the city. The princes and people reject this verdict. The LORD also speaks of his servants the prophets whom he sent persistently, and whom the people did not heed.

l: people of Judah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The people hear Jeremiah, crowd around him, and join in seizing him and demanding his death. After the princes hear the case, the people side with them in declaring he is not worthy of death because he spoke in the LORD's name, and Ahikam keeps him from being given into their hands.

l: princes of Judah and Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The princes of Judah and Jerusalem sit at the new gate's entry, hear the accusation against Jeremiah, and with the people rule he is not worthy of death since he spoke in the LORD's name; they also transgress the servants' liberty covenant.

l: Uriah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Uriah, son of Shemaiah from Kiriath Jearim, was a prophet who prophesied in the LORD's name against the city and land; Jehoiakim sought his death, he fled to Egypt, was brought back, killed, and buried among commoners.

l: Jeremiah's prophecy of destruction, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Jeremiah's conditional prophecy of destruction warns that if the people ignore the LORD's law and prophets, the LORD's house will become like Shiloh and Jerusalem a curse to all nations. It provokes demands for his death, yet allows the LORD to relent if they amend; elders cite Micah's similar prophecy.

l: false prophets (of Judah and the nations), The Book of Jeremiah
s: prophesies lie [telling nations not to serve Babylon's king] Prophets, diviners, dreamers, soothsayers, and sorcerers are said to tell the nations and Judah not to serve the king of Babylon, which the LORD calls a lie meant to remove them from their land and cause them to perish. The LORD says he has not sent them, that they prophesy falsely in his name, and that some claim the temple vessels will soon return from Babylon. Jeremiah challenges them to intercede so the remaining vessels don't go to Babylon.

l: bonds and bars (Jeremiah's yoke), The Book of Jeremiah
s: The LORD instructs Jeremiah to make bonds and bars and put them on his neck. They serve as the sign accompanying the message sent to the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon that they should put their necks under Babylon's yoke.

l: vessels (of the LORD's house), The Book of Jeremiah
s: The vessels of the LORD's house, including pillars, sea, bases, and remaining temple, king's house, and Jerusalem vessels, were not yet taken by Nebuchadnezzar. Prophets falsely promise quick return; the LORD says they will be carried to Babylon until he visits and restores them.

l: Hananiah the son of Azzur, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Hananiah, a prophet from Gibeon, declared in the LORD's house that Babylon's yoke was broken and captives and vessels would return within two years. He broke Jeremiah's neck bar, was told the LORD had not sent him and he promoted a lie, and died that year in the seventh month.
